sections.h2: Which sale routes suit a Chicago owner who wants speed?
sections.html:
Three routes exist: work with a broker, sell it yourself, or accept money from a cash purchaser. A two-flat, a bungalow and a high-rise condo each point toward a different choice, so start with the building's condition and your deadline.

  • Broker listing. Showings come first, then a buyer whose lender sends an appraiser. Inspection findings turn into repair credits or price cuts.
  • Sale by owner. You save the commission and take on pricing, showings and the paperwork, usually with an attorney reviewing the contract.
  • Cash purchase. The purchaser accepts the building as it stands. Expect a lower figure than a polished retail sale and compare it with your net after repairs and carrying costs.

Every route ends with the same public filings: a transfer tax declaration, a recorded deed and a seller disclosure report.

sections.h2: What does Chicago look like in the Census numbers?
sections.html:
Chicago is a very large city made of many separate housing markets, so a street-by-street view matters more than the citywide average. Estimates for mid-2025 put the population at 2,731,585 within 227.73 square miles of land, or about 12,060 people per square mile in the 2020 count.

Chicago received its city charter on March 4, 1837 and rebuilt after the fire of October 8, 1871, which burned an area about four miles long and a mile wide. It sits on the southwestern shore of Lake Michigan and is the seat of Cook County. University of Chicago sociologists divided it into community areas in the late 1920s, and the city now recognizes 77 of them, containing more than 200 informal neighborhoods.

The 2020 to 2024 Census housing figures show how mixed the stock is. Only 46.0 percent of Chicago households own their residence. The middle owner-occupied value is $334,100 and the middle gross rent is $1,440. There are 1,160,205 households averaging 2.29 people.

sections.h2: How much transfer tax does a Chicago sale carry?
sections.html:
Three layers of transfer tax can apply to a Chicago sale: a state tax, a city tax and a surcharge for the Chicago Transit Authority. At the state level, Section 31-10 of the Property Tax Code taxes a transfer at fifty cents per $500 of the value stated in the declaration, or fraction of $500.

The City of Chicago adds its own real property transfer tax. Its Department of Finance prints the rate as $5.25 per $500 of transfer price, made up of a $3.75 city portion and a $1.50 CTA portion. In general the buyer owes the $3.75 and the seller owes the $1.50. Section 3-33-060 of the municipal code lists the exemptions, and the page says none applies unless the declaration describes supporting facts and attaches documents.

Where each piece of Chicago transfer paperwork goes
ItemWhere it is handledSource
Transfer tax declarationFiled online through MyDec; the city does not take declarations by mailChicago Department of Finance
Transfer stampsDepartment of Finance counter at 121 N. LaSalle, Room 107, or a registered title companyChicago Department of Finance
Deed recordingCook County Clerk, Recordings DivisionCook County Clerk
State transfer taxFifty cents per $500 of declared valueReal Estate Transfer Tax Law, Article 31

One break is worth knowing about. The city page describes a refund of the CTA portion for a buyer who is at least 65, lives in the home for a year or more and paid $250,000 or less. Have the title company confirm which lines apply to your contract, since the buyer and seller can agree to split charges differently.

sections.h2: Who records a Chicago deed, and what happens at the filing?
sections.html:
Recording belongs to the Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division, not to City Hall. Its public search finds recorded land documents by property index number and party name.

The counter keeps nine-to-five hours and stops taking customers at 4:45 pm. The Clerk's site also lists a Property Fraud Unit for owners who spot a questionable filing against their home.

At most closings the title company or attorney prepares the declaration, buys the stamps and sends the deed, so a seller seldom needs to go downtown in person.

sections.h2: Which Cook County tax exemptions affect a Chicago house?
sections.html:
Missing exemptions are a common reason a Chicago bill runs high. The Homeowner Exemption subtracts $10,000 from equalized assessed value, continues each year once granted, and the Assessor puts its average saving near $950 a year.

  • Senior Exemption: a further reduction for owners 65 and over who live in the home.
  • Senior Freeze: household income at or under $65,000 for 2024, refiled yearly.
  • Long-Time Homeowner Exemption: about 2 percent of owners qualify, and the Assessor mails applications to likely candidates.
  • Home Improvement Exemption: applied without an application for up to $75,000 of added value, for four years at most.

The second installment bill lists the exemptions applied. If one was missed, a Certificate of Error can recover savings for tax years 2021 through 2025. The 2025 second installment bills were mailed September 1, 2026 and were due October 1, 2026. Mention any pending certificate to whoever runs your closing.

sections.h2: What must a Chicago seller disclose under Illinois law?
sections.html:
A written disclosure report must reach the buyer before a contract is signed. Section 20 of the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act sets the duty and Section 35 prints the form.

Questions on the form that matter in older Chicago housing include basement or crawl space leakage, foundation and roof defects, outdated electrical or plumbing, radon, asbestos, and lead paint or lead service and plumbing pipes. Termites, buried fuel tanks, boundary disputes and open violation notices appear too.

The seller answers from actual knowledge, may still sell as-is, and must update the report if conditions change before closing.

sections.h2: How do Chicago winters and older buildings affect a quick sale?
sections.html:
Four distinct seasons shape Chicago houses: hot, humid summers and winters with real cold and snow. The normal winter high from December through March is about 36 degrees Fahrenheit, and measurable snow can continue into the first or second week of April. Summer heat waves are frequent, though lake breezes keep the shoreline cooler.

Lake Michigan moderates temperatures, so waterfront neighborhoods run slightly warmer in winter and cooler in summer than inland ones. The disclosure form asks directly about basement leakage and roof, wall and foundation defects, so expect buyers to start there.

Before taking any offer, list what an inspector would flag and estimate each repair. A long list favors a buyer who takes the property as-is over a retail listing that may stall on repair credits.

sections.h2: What belongs in a side-by-side check of Chicago offers?
sections.html:
Compare what each offer leaves in your bank account after every cost. Request each proposal in writing with a closing date and a list of who pays what.

  • Which side covers each transfer tax portion, and whether the contract departs from the usual split.
  • Whether open city violations travel with the building.
  • How leases are handled in a multi-unit property.
  • How leftover property tax installments and water balances are settled.
  • Whether the purchaser waives a mortgage contingency and appraisal.

A second offer or a broker's price opinion gives you something to measure against.

faqs.q: How fast can a house sell in Chicago?
faqs.a: Title work, tenants and the speed of the declaration and deed filings set the pace. A cash purchaser removes the lender and appraiser from the timeline.

faqs.q: Who pays the Chicago transfer tax?
faqs.a: Per the Department of Finance, the buyer generally owes $3.75 per $500 and the seller $1.50 per $500. The state tax is separate and the contract may shift either piece, so confirm with your title company.

faqs.q: Do I need to repair my Chicago house before selling?
faqs.a: No. An as-is sale is allowed, but the disclosure report still has to be delivered first. A purchaser who takes the house as-is will price the needed work into the figure.

faqs.q: Where does the deed get filed after a Chicago closing?
faqs.a: The Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division records it, usually through the title company along with the MyDec declaration.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Chicago house that has tenants in it?
faqs.a: Yes. Hand the buyer the leases and rent records, and ask your attorney about deposits and lease handling at closing.
